article.title: Hiring in September grew much less than expected, jobs report shows
article.summary:
Hiring in September grew much less than expected, jobs report showsHiring grew much less than expected in September as a monthslong surge of inflation weighed on shoppers and rattled bond markets, according to the federal government's monthly jobs report.
Employers added 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp slowdown from the 162,000 jobs added in August, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics data showed.
Economists expected employers to have added 84,000 jobs last month.

article.title: How climate change is altering petrichor, the glorious smell after it rains

The distinct, earthy smell that fills the air after rain following a long dry spell can trigger some serious nostalgia.
But as climate change alters Earth’s weather and environment, petrichor is going to transform, too.
During dry periods, soil-dwelling bacteria produce a compound called geosmin that deters insects such as fruit flies.
Droughts cause geosmin to build up, and when they occur with hotter temperatures, bacteria produce even more geosmin as heat speeds up chemical reactions inside the microbes.
But if soils get too dry, “the geosmin will dry up and not be released,” Lundström says.

Amazon’s also simplifying its streaming stick lineup, which now includes four devices instead of five: the Fire TV Stick HD, Fire TV Stick 4K, Fire TV Stick 4K Max, and Fire TV Cube.
The new Fire TV Stick 4K is replacing Amazon’s earlier “Select” and “Plus” 4K streaming sticks.

article.title: 3 Ways Founders Can Protect Margins When Growth Slows
article.summary:
Founders can improve the economics of growth by reducing variation, removing integration friction and turning customer success into a source of recurring value.
Here are three ways founders can make growth more repeatable and protect margins in the process.
Turn customer success into a revenue engineCustomer success is often viewed primarily as a retention function.
Customer success teams can also help expansion happen more naturally.
The bottom lineWhen growth slows, protecting margins does not have to mean indiscriminate cost cutting.

article.title: Supreme Court grants review of Trump administration's mandatory detention policy for immigrants
article.summary:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court on Thursday agreed to review a Trump administration policy denying bond hearings for immigrants as the government carries out a sweeping crackdown.
The case will test a key pillar of the Trump administration's hard-line immigration agenda.
He sought a bond hearing after an immigration judge determined that his detention was mandatory following his September 2025 arrest.

The policy change departs from the practices of prior administrations, which typically allowed most noncitizens without criminal records to request a bond hearing if they were arrested away from the border.

article.title: Family of Renee Good sues ICE agent and top Trump officials
article.summary:
The family of Renee Good, the woman killed by immigration agents in January in Minneapolis, filed two federal lawsuits against the agent who shot her and several top officials in the Trump administration on Thursday.
In the lawsuits, Good's partner, Becca Good, and her brother, Brent Ganger, alleged wrongful death and other violations of federal law, according to a press release issued by their lawyers.
Multiple video clips of the encounter, however, show that Good was steering her vehicle away from the agent as she tried to drive away.
Shortly after Good's killing, Todd Blanche, then the deputy US attorney general, said he saw no grounds for opening a civil rights investigation.
Days later, the justice department opened an investigation into the relationship between Becca Good, the deceased's partner, and protest groups.

article.title: Greece pushes EU to suspend asylum during mass migration surges
article.summary:
Greece has urged the European Union to allow member states to temporarily suspend asylum applications during periods of mass migration, arguing that current rules cannot handle emergencies such as the surge in Spain’s North African enclave of Ceuta this summer.
The proposal was submitted to EU interior ministers meeting in Luxembourg on Thursday during the Justice and Home Affairs Council, and appeared to draw support from some member states.
Greek Migration Minister Thanos Plevris said the EU’s migration pact, which took effect in June, had improved the bloc’s ability to manage migration flows but had not gone far enough.
“In such cases, there should be enhanced border surveillance and suspension of asylum,” he told reporters ahead of the meeting.
Dutch Migration Minister Bart van den Brink backed the approach, saying mass arrivals like those in Ceuta should be “treated as a border management issue rather than an asylum issue”.

article.title: Sunday in Japan: A Ugandan asylum seeker turns to filmmaking
article.summary:
Facing deportation from Japan, a Ugandan filmmaker makes a samurai film inspired by his own life.
For more than 15 years, Sunday, a Ugandan asylum seeker, has lived in limbo in Japan.
Changes to Japan’s immigration laws mean he could face deportation.
Refusing to be reduced to a statistic, Sunday throws himself into an unlikely project: a samurai film inspired by Yasuke, remembered as Japan’s first Black samurai.
Sunday in Japan is a documentary film by Antonio Rui Ribeiro, Leo Nelki and Golriz Kolahi.

The facility will be managed by LaSalle Family Foundation, a nonprofit arm of LaSalle Corrections, a private prison company that manages several immigration detention centers across the country.

Millions could be affectedThe Supreme Court case stems from a 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruling involving Ricardo Aparecido Barbosa da Cunha, a Brazilian national who entered the US around 2004 or 2005.

article.title: Six smugglers jailed for manslaughter over worst Channel small boats disaster
article.summary:
Six people traffickers have been found guilty in France of causing the deaths of 31 migrants in the worst ever small-boat accident in the Channel.
At the end of a four-week trial in Paris, the six were convicted of "involuntary homicide" and given prison terms of between six and 10 years.
Seven others were given lesser sentences of up to four years, and one person was found not guilty.
The boat went down early in the morning on 24 November 2021 after sending distress calls to French and British coastguards.
The dead, including a child of seven, were mainly Iraqi Kurds but also included Afghans, Egyptians and Iranian Kurds.

article.title: French court sentences 13 men over deadliest small-boat crossing to UK
article.summary:
Six people smugglers are found guilty of involuntary homicide after 31 migrants died in the English Channel in 2021.
A French court has sentenced 13 men to up to 10 years in prison for their roles in the deadliest small-boat crossing by migrants trying to reach the United Kingdom from France.
The court in Paris found six of the men guilty of involuntary homicide on Wednesday, handing down prison terms of between six and 10 years.
The remaining seven men were found guilty of lesser criminal charges and were sentenced to up to four years in jail.
The court said the smugglers were driven by greed and were “profiting from the vulnerability of exile candidates”.

article.summary:
The two lawsuits – filed on Thursday by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee’s brother, Brent Ganger – say officials from US President Donald Trump’s administration were reckless and violated the civil rights of Good and others in Minneapolis.
The lawsuits are the first major civil actions taken against the Trump administration over its unprecedented deportation crackdowns in Minneapolis last winter, dubbed Operation Metro Surge.
Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defence and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism”.
Minnesota sued the Trump administration in March to gain access to the evidence it gathered at the shooting scenes, but investigations stalled after the Justice Department halted its routine cooperation and evidence-sharing with the Minneapolis Police Department.
None of the agents involved in Good’s killing has faced any charges.

article.title: Putin shows no sign of stopping the war as Russia doubles down on Ukraine
article.summary:
When Vladimir Putin arrived to address Russia's parliament on Wednesday, a warm welcome was guaranteed.
"The Special Election Operation", as one Russian newspaper dubbed last month's legislative vote, has produced a State Duma even more pro-Putin than anything before it.
Are there any signs he is prepared to halt what he calls the special military operation?
Right now, everything points to Putin continuing Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine: despite his country's huge battlefield losses to date and the damage being done to Russia's economy.
Putin's speeches and statements suggest he remains confident that Russia can secure a military victory.

article.title: California man smuggled $300 million in Nvidia chips to China, prosecutors say
article.summary:
A California man is facing federal charges for helping smuggle over $300 million worth of Nvidia semiconductor chips into China, prosecutors said this week.
It is illegal to export advanced semiconductor chips into China without a license, as the US competes with the East Asian giant in the AI race.
President Donald Trump drew criticism last year for allowing Nvidia to sell its chips to China, a departure from the previous US policy under President Joe Biden, which effectively blocked all exports of advanced chips to China.

article.title: Suspected Chinese spies spoofed an Anthropic exec, ex-White House official in AI phishing
article.summary:
A suspected Chinese espionage group impersonated AI policy figures, including a senior Anthropic employee and a former White House official, in phishing campaigns targeting AI policy experts at US universities, think tanks, and law firms, security researchers say.
REG AD“In July 2026, TA419 impersonated multiple individuals, including a former member of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy leadership team, in credential phishing campaigns targeting AI policy experts in the US,” Proofpoint threat-intelligence analyst Mark Kelly said in a Thursday report.
The suspected spies’ emails invited their targets to join a fake AI policy advisory committee or contribute to a Senate foreign relations committee report on AI export controls and supply chains.
In February - as US military officials pressured Anthropic to remove Claude’s safeguards - the Chinese spies spoofed a senior Anthropic employee to phish an AI policy analyst at a US think tank.

article.title: SoftBank completes $30bn OpenAI investment with final $10bn payment
article.summary:
SoftBank Group has completed its $30bn follow-on investment in OpenAI, after paying the third and final $10bn tranche on 1 October, Japan time.
The Japanese group made the payment through its Vision Fund 2, it said on Thursday.
With this payment, SoftBank has now put $64.6bn into OpenAI in total, for a stake of about 13%.
To cover the final tranche, SoftBank used the proceeds of a foreign-currency bond sale announced on 24 September.
Before the latest commitment, SoftBank had already invested $34.6bn in OpenAI through Vision Fund 2 since September 2024.

article.summary:

In 2023, Evan Gershkovich was working as a young reporter in Moscow for the Wall Street Journal, when he was arrested by Russian authorities.
He was eventually convicted on blatantly false charges of espionage and spent nearly five hundred days in imprisonment.
Gershkovich recounts the experience in a new memoir, “This Cursed Beautiful Land,” and in an essay in The New Yorker.
He spoke with David Remnick about life inside a Russian prison, the international prisoner swap that freed him, and why the difficult process of reacclimating to his former life complicated how he viewed his incarceration.

article.title: Schneier on Security
article.summary:
Unidentified Flock Cameras in FloridaSt. Lucie County in Florida discovered (alt link) a dozen Flock cameras whose ownership it can’t identify, and that the county government had not permitted.
I am reminded of the decade-old story of StingRay cell phone surveillance devices in Washington, DC, whose operators were also unknown.
My guess is that in the StingRay case, the devices were operated by foreign actors.
This Flock case is more likely some local government entity that didn’t bother getting approval.
Were I a foreign actor, I would rather hack the existing Flock network—like Israel did with Tehran’s surveillance cameras—than risk installing my own.
